summary: Documents methods applications use to set up direct peer-to-peer communication through Network Address Translators. It is mostly descriptive, with advisory security recommendations. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5128 records the methods applications use to connect directly to each other when a router in between rewrites addresses. It explains how a NAT decides which packets to let in, then describes relaying, connection reversal, hole punching and port prediction, with the security risks each one carries.

questions: how do peers connect through nat
subtitle: The tricks applications use to talk directly to each other when a router rewrites their addresses.

tldr.problem: A router that translates addresses hides the real address of every machine behind it, so a peer outside cannot open a connection to it. Peer-to-peer applications need a way around that.
tldr.mechanism: The document describes the known methods: relaying through a rendezvous server, connection reversal, UDP and TCP hole punching, and port number prediction, together with the mapping and filtering behaviour of a NAT that decides which of them can work.
tldr.outcome: Hole punching is the most efficient method and works on most deployed NATs, but it needs an endpoint-independent mapping NAT, so applications still need a relaying fallback.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
Network Address Translators (NATs) are deployed throughout the Internet, in a variety of device types and network topologies. The asymmetric addressing and connectivity they create cause real problems for peer-to-peer applications such as teleconferencing and multiplayer online gaming. The document expects the problems to persist into the IPv6 world: during the transition some form of NAT may be needed so that IPv4-only nodes can talk to IPv6-only nodes, and even a future pure IPv6 world may still include firewalls whose filtering behaviour resembles a NAT's without the address translation.

Deployed NAT devices are built around the client/server model, where relatively anonymous client machines inside a private network initiate connections to public servers with stable addresses and DNS names. The illusion of anonymity and inaccessibility is no problem for a Web browser, which only needs to initiate outgoing connections. In the peer-to-peer model, hosts that would be considered clients also accept sessions from peers. The initiator and the responder may sit behind different NAT devices, with neither endpoint holding a permanent address or any other public presence. A common online gaming architecture has every host register with a publicly addressable rendezvous server and discover other hosts there, then establish direct connections between themselves. A file sharing application works the same way, using a well-known server for discovery and direct connections for the data.

The document summarizes the known methods applications use to work around NATs without altering the NAT devices themselves. It covers TCP and UDP applications only, and it is restricted to establishing two-way communication between endpoints. Techniques that involve explicit signalling between applications and NAT devices, such as NAT-PMP, SOCKS, RSIP and UPnP, are out of scope, though they are complementary. The document is descriptive and is not an endorsement of the methods it records.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that translates addresses gives each machine behind it a private address that the rest of the Internet cannot reach. Web browsing works because the computer only ever starts conversations. Peer-to-peer software is different, because both sides have to be able to start one. This document lists the ways that has been solved.

sections.title: How a NAT Maps and Filters Traffic
sections.content:
An endpoint is a session-specific tuple on a host; for UDP or TCP it is an IP address and port number. When a host inside a private realm starts a session to a host in the public realm, the NAT assigns a public endpoint to stand in for the private one, so that reply packets can be received, translated and forwarded. That assignment is called endpoint mapping.

Endpoint-independent mapping means the NAT reuses the same port mapping for subsequent packets sent from the same internal address and port to any external address and port. Endpoint-dependent mapping covers the address-dependent case, where the mapping is reused for the same external IP address regardless of its port, and the address-and-port-dependent case, where the mapping is reused only for the same external IP address and port while the mapping is active.

Filtering decides which incoming packets the NAT lets through. With endpoint-independent filtering the NAT forwards any packet destined to the mapped internal address and port, whatever the external source, so sending a packet out to any external address is enough to allow packets back. With endpoint-dependent filtering the NAT also drops packets from an external endpoint the internal host has never contacted. The combination of endpoint-independent mapping and endpoint-independent filtering is a NAT that accepts incoming traffic to a mapped public port from any external endpoint; the document calls a NAT that uses endpoint-independent mapping an EIM-NAT, whatever its filtering behaviour. A further term is hairpinning: when two hosts sit behind the same NAT, the NAT may allocate an outside address for one of them and relay traffic from the other back into the private network, because packets arriving from inside are translated and looped back rather than passed out to the public network. Not all deployed NATs support it.
sections.plainLanguage: Two decisions decide what a translator allows. The first is mapping: does the same outside port number get reused for everything a machine sends, or does a fresh port number get handed out per destination. The second is filtering: will packets from a stranger be accepted, or only from addresses the machine has already talked to. Hole punching depends on the first decision being the first kind.

sections.title: Relaying and Connection Reversal
sections.content:
Relaying is the most reliable and least efficient method. It makes the peer-to-peer traffic look like client/server traffic to the network. Two hosts behind NATs each open a connection to a publicly addressable rendezvous server S, which is used for registration, discovery and relay. To send a message to client B, client A sends it to S along the connection A already has, and S forwards it to B over the connection it already has with B. The method always works as long as both clients can reach the server, and the NAT on the way does not have to be an EIM-NAT. The costs are the server's processing power and network bandwidth, and extra latency between the peers. The TURN protocol defines an application-agnostic, session-oriented, relatively secure form of packet relay.

Connection reversal works only when one peer is behind a NAT and the other is not. A client A behind NAT A has private address 10.0.0.1 and uses TCP port 1234. Its connection to server S at 192.0.2.128 port 20001 has been given the public endpoint 192.0.2.1:62000 by NAT A, so S believes A is at that address. Client B has a permanent address, 192.0.2.254, and listens on port 1234. If B tries to reach A at 10.0.0.1:1234 the traffic is dropped, because that address is not publicly routable, and if B tries 192.0.2.1:62000 the SYN arrives at NAT A and is rejected, because only outgoing connections are allowed.

After failing to connect directly, B can ask S to relay a request to A, and A then opens a connection to B at B's public address and port. NAT A permits it because the connection starts inside the firewall, and B accepts it because B is not behind a NAT. The limitation is obvious: it works only while at most one of the two peers is behind a NAT. If the NAT is an EIM-NAT, the public client can ask S which public endpoint to expect the connection from and accept connections from only that endpoint; if it is not an EIM-NAT, the public client cannot know which endpoint to expect. In the increasingly common case where both peers sit behind NATs, the method fails, and applications fall back to relaying.
sections.plainLanguage: Relaying makes the two peers talk through a public server instead of to each other. It always works but puts the traffic on the server. Connection reversal is cleverer: the peer that has a public address asks the server to tell the hidden peer to call it instead. That works only while one of the two peers has a public address.

sections.title: Hole Punching
sections.content:
UDP hole punching relies on the properties of EIM-NATs. When one host is behind a NAT that is not an EIM-NAT, the peering host cannot predictably know the mapped endpoint to connect to, and the host behind the non-EIM-NAT cannot reuse an established mapping for a different destination, so the technique fails.

Consider two clients A and B behind different NATs, each using UDP port 1234, with a rendezvous server S on UDP port 20001. NAT A has assigned public port 62000 to A's session with S, and NAT B has assigned port 31000 to B's session with S. If A simply starts sending UDP messages to B's public endpoint 192.0.2.254:31000, NAT B will typically discard them, because the source address and port do not match those of S with which the original session was established. The same happens in the other direction.

So A starts sending to B's public endpoint and at the same time relays a request through S asking B to send to A's public endpoint. A's outgoing messages cause EIM-NAT A to open a new session between A's private endpoint and B's public endpoint, and B's messages cause EIM-NAT B to open a new session between B's private endpoint and A's public endpoint. With both new sessions open, the two clients talk directly and S is left with the role of an introduction server. Once a direct connection exists, either party can act as introducer for further peers, which lowers the load on S. The application does not need to detect what kind of NAT it is behind, and the technique works with multiple NATs in the path.

When two clients are behind the same NAT, hairpinning applies: A's packet to B's public endpoint is translated by the NAT and looped back into the private network, which adds latency and burdens the NAT. The fix is to exchange both the private and the public addresses through S and to send packets to every candidate address at once, using the first that works. The packets must be authenticated in some way, because a packet aimed at a private address can reach an unrelated host on the local network.

TCP hole punching, also called Simultaneous TCP Open, works the same way. Two endpoints may start a TCP session by simultaneously sending SYN packets, each replying with a separate ACK, a procedure found in figure 6 of the original TCP specification, though it is not implemented correctly on many systems including NAT devices. If a NAT receives a SYN from outside for a session it believes is already active, it lets the packet through, so if each client's outgoing SYN passes its own NAT before either SYN reaches the far NAT, a working connection results. It fails when a SYN arrives at the remote NAT too quickly, before the other side has sent its own, because the remote NAT may drop it or answer with a RST. In practice, more than 50% of NAT devices support endpoint-independent mapping and do not send ICMP errors or RSTs in response to unsolicited SYNs, so the technique works across NAT devices in the majority of TCP connection attempts.
sections.plainLanguage: Hole punching works because each side sends a packet out to the other's outside address at the same moment. The translator sees outgoing traffic to that address and lets return traffic through. Each side ends up with a direct path to the other, and the server that introduced them steps out of the way.

sections.title: Port Prediction, Other Protocols and Measured Results
sections.content:
UDP port number prediction, sometimes called the N+1 technique, allows a peer-to-peer UDP session to be created across NATs that use endpoint-dependent mapping. It works by predicting the public port numbers the NAT will assign to future sessions, which is often possible because most NATs assign mapping ports in sequence. In the worked example, NAT A has assigned port 62000 to A's session with S and NAT B has assigned port 31000 to B's session with S. Client A starts sending to port 31001 at 192.0.2.254 and client B starts sending to port 62001 at 192.0.2.1, hoping each NAT hands out the next port in sequence. The trick fails if the predicted port is already in use, if a NAT sometimes picks ports non-sequentially, or if another client behind the same NAT opens a connection in between and takes the desired port. It is therefore much less likely to work when the NAT is under load, and it has little chance of working when a client is behind two or more levels of NAT. TCP port number prediction is the same idea for TCP and is even more fragile, because a wrongly predicted port or a SYN that arrives too early and draws a RST can close the new session and make further SYN retransmissions with the same ports futile.

Other work covered in the document includes ICE, which exchanges several candidate endpoints between peers during an offer and answer exchange and selects the most efficient ones; Teredo, which tunnels packets over UDP to a relay node so that IPv4 hosts behind NATs can reach IPv6 hosts outside; and the practice of using several rendezvous servers for registration, discovery and relay. Applications that use these techniques include online gaming, media over IP and instant messaging.

The measured results are the practical summary. Testing across commercial NAT devices showed that UDP hole punching works widely, on more than 80% of the devices, while TCP hole punching works on just over 60% of them. TCP or UDP hairpinning is not yet widely available: less than 25% of the devices passed the hairpinning tests. More sophisticated techniques than the standard ones raise the share of deployed NATs that can support TCP hole punching to up to 88%.
sections.plainLanguage: When a translator hands out a fresh port number per destination, one peer can guess the number the other will get next and aim there. It works only when the guess is right, which gets harder when the translator is busy. The measurements in the document show hole punching works on most devices, while hairpinning, where two machines behind the same router talk to each other through it, is rare.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document says it creates no new security issues of its own, but the techniques it describes carry risks. Because applications deal with several address domains without knowing the topology, packets sent while setting up a connection often arrive at a host other than the intended one. Consumer NATs hand out addresses by DHCP, and a host at 192.168.1.101 on one home network sending a discovery packet to 192.168.1.100 on another network will reach some other machine on its own network. This aliasing risk exists without any attacker. The advice is to treat any address as suspect until authenticated two-way communication is established.

For denial of service, applications and servers must not take any action needing significant local processing or storage until authenticated two-way communication exists, and must limit the amount and rate of traffic sent to a newly discovered address. An attacker can register a target's IP address with the rendezvous server as if it were its own, drawing connection attempts at it; the server cannot verify the addresses, because they may be legitimate private addresses, so the application protocol must size and rate-limit traffic to unverified addresses.

For man-in-the-middle attacks, any device on the path to the rendezvous server can pretend to be a NAT. An attacker who sees a registration request can flood the server with copies of it carrying the attacker's own source address, so the server registers the client at the attacker's address, putting the attacker in the path of all later traffic. The client cannot defend itself by authenticating its source address, because a NAT-friendly application must let intervening translators change it silently. The only defence is to authenticate and possibly encrypt the content of the communication using higher-level identities.

Finally, the document argues that designing NAT devices to preserve endpoint identities does not weaken their security. Filtering incoming traffic aggressively with endpoint-dependent filtering while using endpoint-independent mapping lets a NAT be friendly to applications without giving up the rejection of unsolicited traffic. Endpoint-independent mapping does make the traffic emerging from the NAT more predictable, which might help an attacker exploit other weaknesses, and a deployment that cares about that should instead restrict which applications and ports may originate traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: These techniques let a peer send packets that may reach the wrong machine, because two private networks can hand out the same address. The advice is to authenticate the connection before doing anything expensive, to limit what is sent to an address nobody has confirmed, and to encrypt the content, since nothing stops a device on the path from posing as the translator.

items.title: Relaying
items.text: The server carries every message between the peers. Always works, costs server bandwidth and adds latency.

items.title: Connection reversal
items.text: The peer with a public address asks the hidden peer to call it. Works only if one peer has a public address.

items.title: UDP hole punching
items.text: Both peers send to each other's outside address at once. Needs endpoint-independent mapping.

items.title: TCP hole punching
items.text: Simultaneous TCP Open, the SYN packets cross in flight. Fails if a SYN arrives before the other is sent.

items.title: UDP port prediction
items.text: Guess the next port number the NAT will hand out. Fails when the guess is wrong or the NAT is busy.

items.title: TCP port prediction
items.text: The same guess for TCP, and even more timing sensitive.
